1:
Hear, O Israel marks a break: Gill supposes a pause after the preceding discourse, Henry and Wesley a new address on the next sabbath. Clarke fixes the moment: this day means this time, they having come near the verge of the land thirty-eight years before and been refused the crossing for their rebellions. He dates the speech to the eleventh month of the fortieth year and the crossing to the month following — and notes that Moses died between. Henry draws out the striking thing. The nations to be dispossessed are mightier than Israel, no undisciplined rout but a people with fortified cities and men great and tall, of whom report said there was no standing before them. That, Henry observes, is nearly the report the evil spies brought back; the difference lies wholly in the intention. Theirs was to drive the people from God and discourage their hope, this to drive them to God and engage it, no power short of almighty being able to prosper them. Wesley says the same in a line: mightier is added so they should not trust their own strength, and when the work was done should ascribe the glory to God.

Keil identifies the enemy Moses is really fighting, and it is not Canaanite. Besides the vulgar pride that forgets God and credits success to its own exertion, there is a subtler kind which acknowledges God's blessings but, instead of receiving them gratefully as unmerited gifts, sees in them only proofs of its own righteousness. That is the danger Moses warns against, declaring outright that Canaan is not given for Israel's righteousness but taken from the Canaanites for theirs. Henry notices Moses says it three times over — not for thy righteousness, not for the uprightness of thy heart, neither for thy good conversation nor thy good disposition — because it is hard to bring people off a conceit of their merit and yet necessary that it be done. Had entry hung on that condition, Israel had been shut out for ever, being a stiffnecked people. The two real reasons are drawn from God's honour: he will be honoured in destroying idolaters, and in performing the promise sworn to the patriarchs. From which Henry states the asymmetry as sharply as it can be put — all whom God rejects are rejected for their own wickedness, but none whom he accepts are accepted for their own righteousness.

Calvin reads the passage as a eulogy on God's gratuitous liberality. That Israel should inherit Canaan by no merit of their own but by signal bounty, flowing wholly from the covenant and their free adoption, ought to have been a pressing stimulus, ravishing them to the worship of a God they owed so much; it were disgraceful that men whom grace had gone before should not meet him willingly. To leave them nothing to arrogate, Moses magnifies the difficulty: the nations excelled in numbers and valour, their cities were impregnable, and among them were the children of Anak. He cites the people as witnesses, the report having so terrified them they wished to turn back. The giants, Calvin notes, were known to few — whom thou knowest, and of whom thou hast heard points to the spies — but Moses transfers the case of a few to them all, their report having spread terror through the camp as though they had already met them in the field. He convicts them on their own evidence lest they later claim the praise due to God; and the lesson, he adds, is that such is the ingratitude of mankind that men obscure God's bounties as far as they can, and never yield except when driven to conviction. Ellicott glosses fenced up to heaven by the tower whose top was in the heavens, and wonders whether Paul had it in mind writing of wrestling against wickedness in heavenly places.
2:
Ellicott hears a structure here built on one repeated word. Three times the formula occurs: the children of Anak thou knowest, thou knowest the Lord thy God, and thou knowest thyself. The pronouns are emphatic — whom thou knowest, of giants the spies had seen, of whom it seems to have been a common saying, perhaps among the Anakim themselves, that none would stand up to them; and again, not for thy righteousness dost thou go, the force being that there is no reason why thou shouldst be so honoured. Gill glosses it simply, a people of large bulk and stature beside whom the spies seemed grasshoppers. Against that stands the promise of a Lord who goes over as a consuming fire, and Calvin will not have the figure misread. Elsewhere God is so called in another sense, that we may fear his wrath; here Moses means only that the destruction of these nations was God's wonderful work, the similitude heightening the miracle, since no ordinary means could have made so many warlike peoples perish so quickly. Keil ties the halves together grammatically: when Jehovah thrusts these nations out, Israel is not to say within itself that it is for their righteousness — the following clause being adversative, but for the nations' wickedness.

Calvin's exposition of speak not in thine heart is the most careful here. To speak in the heart is to reflect, so that Moses reproves not the boasting of the lips but the hidden arrogance by which men take to themselves the praise due to God. He then makes a distinction easy to miss. Moses does not merely forbid them to think they took the land unaided; he assumes they will grant the victory was God's, but is not content with that limited gratitude unless they also own that they deserved nothing of the kind, so that it was a mere and gratuitous act of bounty. God is not less defrauded, Calvin adds, when men set their righteousness against his liberality than when they boast their blessings got by their own industry. He then admits a weakness. That the nations were driven out for wickedness is not on its face conclusive, since God might take from reprobates only to give to worthier men; so Calvin reads it as an indirect admonition to compare themselves with those nations, from which, knowing themselves poor and miserable, they could conclude they had not earned a foreign land.

Clarke pushes the reasoning furthest. These peoples were cast out not by a sovereign act but for their wickedness; they had transgressed their Creator's law, resisted his Spirit, and could no longer be tolerated. Israel possessed it not by desert but because they were less wicked, and because God chose to begin the work of salvation among men there. The Canaanites were cut off and Israel grafted in — and Israel, for their wickedness, cut off afterwards and the Gentiles grafted in, so let these not be high-minded but fear. Yet the land was originally the Canaanites' own, Clarke adds, and the new possessors had no legal right. On the stiffnecked people the pictures differ: Calvin takes the metaphor from oxen, useless until taught to bend the neck, so the people not merely refused submission but shook off the yoke; Ellicott takes it from a camel that hardens its neck and will not bend for the driver. Calvin adds the decisive chronology — the covenant was made with Abraham almost four centuries before these men were born, so the benefit came from elsewhere; and if God so exalts his mercy over an earthly inheritance, how much less will he bear men obtruding merits to acquire heaven. Wesley reaches it in a sentence: neither upright heart nor holy life, the two things God most regards, so all merit is excluded — they who did not deserve an earthly Canaan could not merit glory.
7:
Remember, and forget not — the Hebrew is blunter, Ellicott says: remember, forget not, how thou hast stirred the indignation of Jehovah. He presses the word rendered rebellious, which is not simply rebels, as Moses called them at Meribah, but provoking rebels, who rouse the opposition of him against whom they rebel. Gill notes with Aben Ezra that the provoking did not begin after Horeb: they murmured for water at Marah when three days in the wilderness, for bread in the wilderness of Sin, and again at Rephidim, all before Sinai. Henry makes the purpose plain. Lest they think God brought them to Canaan for their righteousness, Moses shows it a miracle of mercy they were not destroyed long since — so far from purchasing his favour, they had often laid themselves open to his displeasure. Their fathers' provocations are charged on this generation, since had God dealt with the fathers by desert these men had never existed, much less entered Canaan. We are apt to forget our provocations, Henry adds, especially once the smart of the rod is over, and need reminding lest we entertain any conceit of our own righteousness — which is Paul's argument from the guilt of all mankind: if our works condemn us, they will not justify us.

Calvin explains why the story is retold, and in almost the words Moses used in Exodus. It is to reprove ingratitude: he touches on several offences but dwells on the revolt, in which their most detestable impiety betrayed itself, and urges them to reflect often on their sins, since constant recollection not only humbles but teaches men at length to lay aside their depraved nature and grow accustomed to obedience. On the harder question he will not speculate. If it is asked how Moses prevailed on God to change his intention, curiosity must be repressed, lest we dispute further than is fitting about a secret and incomprehensible decree. God did not act otherwise than he had determined; Moses goes no deeper than the sentence revealed to him — and so must we, assured that destruction is prepared for us when we transgress and that God's anger is appeased when we fly to his mercy in true faith.

What makes the calf so grievous is when and where it was done. Keil marks the grammar: the connecting particle brings the sin into prominence as specially heinous — and indeed even in Horeb ye provoked Jehovah — heinous for its circumstances. Moses had gone up and stayed forty days, occupied with the holiest things, neither eating nor drinking, to receive tables written with the finger of God in the very words the Lord had spoken to the people out of the fire; at a time when Israel should have been meditating on what they had just heard, they departed at once from the way pointed out and made a molten image. Wesley piles up the same aggravations: their deliverance from Egypt was fresh in memory, God had newly manifested himself in a manner stupendous and dreadful, had just taken them into covenant, and was then conferring further mercies. Ellicott compresses it to a line — in the very sight of the mountain of the Law, the Law was flagrantly violated — and notes that Moses neither eating bread nor drinking water during the first forty days is nowhere related in Exodus, where he goes up with his minister Joshua. It might be supposed, but it is not recorded. On the tables Gill dwells on how wholly they were God's work: the letters of his devising, the writing his, the engraving his own doing, which stamped divine authority on the law and denoted its duration. Wesley draws the lesson — the finger of God signifies not only that greater reverence was due the law, but that it is God's work alone to write it on the tables of men's hearts.
11:
The news comes down before Moses does. Gill points the irony: the omniscient God knew what was doing in the camp though Moses did not, and told him. Clarke glosses the charge — they had debased themselves by making and worshipping an Egyptian idol. Ellicott notes the words summarised here stand at length in Exodus, where Moses's intercession is also recorded. Then Let me alone, that I may destroy them, on which Wesley is briefest: stop me not by thy intercession. Gill reads it likewise, as a command not to say one word on their behalf. What strikes Ellicott hardest is the speed of the fall. On ye had turned aside quickly he writes that nothing in human experience is so sad as the rapidity with which good resolutions and impressions fade from the natural heart of man — words spoken by Jehovah on the mountain, repeated by Moses when he came down, and standing already in Exodus.

The breaking of the tables none of them will call a loss of temper. Ellicott argues it was deliberate: Moses did not drop them in passion before reaching the camp, but broke the material covenant before a people who had broken the covenant itself. Remembering what came in later times of touching not the tables but the chest that held them, he thinks it may have been necessary for Israel's safety; and he notes Moses pitched the temporary tabernacle outside the camp at the same time, the two acts seeming of one significance. Calvin makes the point sharper. Moses accuses himself of no transgression, so we are not to think excessive anger urged him; he repeats what the people deserved and discharges the office of a herald — Calvin has in mind the Roman fecial casting a bloody spear into another's territory to declare war — denouncing by solemn rite, not by word only, that God's covenant was broken by their perfidy, and doing it before their eyes so that, alarmed by so awful a punishment, they might the more earnestly expiate their sin. Wesley agrees: not by unbridled passion but in zeal for God's honour and by his Spirit's direction.

On the forty days Calvin is the chronologist. The order is confused, he says, since this fast did not precede the second ascent — else Moses had fasted three times, which other passages show he did not — and prayers were interposed that are not distinctly recorded here. He insists too on what the fast was not. It was no sign of mourning, as when Joel calls the people to sackcloth and weeping, since abstinence was no more grievous to Moses than to angels; it means that so great a sin could not be expiated unless he again renounced the life of men and was taken up to God. The fear of the next verse Calvin separates from the fast: God had been propitiated already in some measure, calling Moses up to receive the law a second time being itself a token of reconcilement, yet he remained anxious while God did not cease to menace them. Ellicott adds that Joshua was with Moses the first forty days but not the second, and observes that the words rendered I was afraid are in Greek identical with the I exceedingly fear of Hebrews. Aaron closes the passage. Calvin sees in his excuse how vain are the pretexts by which men hide their faults until fear of God subdues them: he did not claim innocence but tried to extenuate the enormity by pleading compulsion, and the greatness of the threatened punishment proves how gross the sin was. The calf is itself called the sin of the people, by metonymy, because it had been the matter and object of their idolatry — and grinding it to powder and casting it into the stream shows how abominable it was, no memorial being suffered to remain.
21:
Moses calls the calf their sin, and both Gill and Ellicott stop on the phrase. Gill takes it as the object of the sin, which lay in making and worshipping it; Ellicott sees the identifying of sin with the object as of a piece with the law in Leviticus, where sin and sin-offering are denoted by one word. Then comes the observation that lifts the verse. The dust was cast into the brook descending out of the mount — and that stream from the rock in Horeb not only gave Israel drink but bore their sin away on its waters; and that Rock, he adds, was Christ. Wesley states the plainer purpose: that no monument of it might be left. Keil takes up the roll of places and finds design in the order. Israel roused the anger of the Lord not at Horeb only but again and again — at Taberah by discontent with God's guidance, at Massah by murmuring for water, at the graves of lust by longing for flesh, at Kadesh-barnea by unbelief. The list is not chronological, he observes, but advances by degrees from the slighter to the graver forms of guilt, to sharpen the people's consciences.

Gill worries at the same disorder without resolving it neatly. The places are not named in the order they happened, Massah coming before Sinai and Taberah after; Aben Ezra reports some who identify the two, but Gill objects that Taberah cannot be the Massah in Rephidim, that lying on one side of the mount and Taberah on the other — though both might bear the name from the tempting done there. He would rather identify Taberah with Kibroth-hattaavah, where the people died with the flesh in their mouths, since no removal between them is recorded and only the latter appears in the itinerary. Ellicott turns the disorder into design: Taberah is the first place named after Sinai, Massah the last scene described before it, so Sinai is made the centre of provocation. Calvin reads the list morally. Moses touches on several cases to convince them of ingratitude and obstinacy, as if to say they rebelled not once nor in one way but heaped offence on offence, so that it is a wonder God pardoned them; and the names of those places stand as memorials of their sins, that they might at length cease to transgress, having been borne with too long.

How many forty-day fasts there were, they cannot agree. Gill reports Jarchi's view that this is the fast already mentioned, repeated for the order of the prayer, notes that at the first is not in the text, and inclines with the Jewish writers and Lightfoot to a third forty days. Calvin holds the narrative simply blended: the prayer was offered before the second fast, but because Moses continued the same petitions while still anxious, he folds into the forty days whatever went before — there being no absurdity in a man still trembling after obtaining the safety he asked. He infers the fast came after the prayer from the next chapter, where the second tables are given with no word of fasting. Ellicott reads the clause as pointing back to the fortieth day, when the Lord told him of the calf. On the prayer Ellicott notices the pronouns, which are the argument in miniature: God had said to Moses thy people, which thou broughtest out, have corrupted themselves — and Moses answers, why doth thy wrath wax hot against thy people, which thou hast brought forth. Clarke dwells on the appeal to the patriarchs, as if Moses said these are their descendants and the covenant was made on these men's behalf; from which he draws that God bestows many blessings on worthless persons for the sake of pious ancestors, or of the religious people they are joined to — so that union with the church is no common blessing.
